newsitem.title: SLOVAK REPUBLIC: Slovak PM blames U.S. for expected NATO failure.
newsitem.headline: Slovak PM blames U.S. for expected NATO failure.

text.p: Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar said on Tuesday that Slovakia had virtually no chance of joining a first phase of NATO expansion and blamed the "negative attitude" of the United States.

Slovakia has often said it wanted to be among the first wave of new members to join the alliance, but its chances appear to have waned in recent months after repeated U.S. and European Union criticism of the pace of its democratic reforms.
"We are disappointed with Slovakia because it did not carry out the type of economic and political reform which we all expected," the U.S. State Department said last week.

"With regard to the negative attitude of the U.S., it makes it very unlikely that Slovakia will be in the first wave of NATO applicants," Meciar told a joint news conference with visiting Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
NATO is to decide at a summit in Madrid in July which former Soviet bloc states it will invite to join its ranks. The Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary are considered leading candidates.

Chernomyrdin, on the second day of a three-day official visit to Bratislava, said Russia remained steadfastly opposed to the expansion of the alliance. He added that he did not want it to become a dominant issue in Russian-Slovak relations.
When asked if Russia would prefer Slovak neutrality, Chernomyrdin said: "From what I have said, it means that we would support any solutions oriented this way."

Moscow, which opposes the expansion, has demanded the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation should not station nuclear and other weapons in new member states and wants a binding treaty on relations between Russia and the alliance.
"We have nothing against NATO, but its military part, which is too dangerous...Nuclear weapons remain pointed at the East," Chernomyrdin said.
He denied claims made by Meciar earlier this year that NATO and Russia had reached a secret pact which excluded Slovakia from having a chance of being in the first round of applicants.
"We stick to our attitude to NATO enlargement, and that's the most important thing to us. We are not interested in who should or should not enter the alliance," Chernomyrdin said.
